intro: Every year, some of the money we pay in taxes leaves town as interest. And some of it already sits in shared accounts. This page starts from those real numbers, then lays out how a community fund can grow, what it can own to lower what families pay, and how it stays honest — with a real example of each.

leaving.title: The money that leaves
leaving.lead: Interest is the price of borrowing. It goes to whoever lent the money — mostly bond investors, anywhere in the country. These are the amounts in local governments’ own bond papers.

rows.what: Arkadelphia School District — new high school bonds, 2027–2056
Arkadelphia School District — 2021 and 2022 bonds, still owed at June 30, 2024
Clark County — Truck Bypass road bonds, over their life

leaving.total: At least $49.3 million of interest leaves these three bond deals alone — before the city’s bonds and bank loans, which aren’t added here.

already.title: What we already pool
already.lead: Shared money isn’t a new idea here. It already exists — in bank accounts and in a sales tax the county dedicates to one purpose.

rows.what: Clark County — money on deposit, Dec 31, 2023
Arkadelphia School District — money on deposit, June 30, 2024
City of Arkadelphia — money on deposit, Dec 31, 2024

rows.note: A pooled fund for economic development. What it paid for isn’t public yet (Docket #5).

src.page: Schedule 2, p. 31 (2023); each earlier year in its own county audit, listed on the Taxes & debt page

already.note: Deposits are from different dates and include money set aside by law, money owed to others, and cash for everyday bills — not all of it is spare. The point is scale: these governments already hold tens of millions of dollars in common.

grow_lead: Arkansas law keeps county and city money out of the stock market (only safe securities of five years or less). That’s fine — the biggest returns for a community fund come from somewhere else.

levers.title: Stop paying interest
levers.body: The surest return is money that no longer leaves. Saving first, or borrowing for fewer years, keeps it here.

precedents.name: Alaska Permanent Fund
precedents.fact: By law, Alaska may draw only 5% a year of the fund’s average value; the rest keeps growing. That draw now supplies over half of the state’s unrestricted general-fund revenue, plus a yearly dividend to residents ($1,000 in 2025).

levers.here: The new high school costs $74.5 million over 30 years. At the same interest rate, paid with the district’s full debt tax, it would take about 7 years and cost about $44 million. Saved for first, about 6 years and $38 million.
levers.limit: Saving first means waiting for the building, and the full debt tax isn’t free until the older bonds are paid.

levers.title: Lend to ourselves
levers.body: A community fund can lend to its own projects and charge itself interest. The interest comes back into the fund instead of leaving.

precedents.name: State revolving funds for water
precedents.fact: Water and sewer loans are repaid with interest into the same fund, which lends it out again. Federal seed money of about $21 billion has turned into more than $41 billion of help this way (through 2019).

precedents.name: Bank of North Dakota
precedents.fact: Opened July 28, 1919 — the only state-owned bank in the nation. State money is deposited with it and lent back into the state.

levers.here: Arkansas already runs revolving loan funds that reach local water and sewer systems. A local fund could work the same way — the details of what Arkansas law lets counties, cities, and school districts lend each other are still being checked.
levers.limit: A revolving fund only works if loans get repaid; a fund that forgives its own loans shrinks.

levers.title: Own what lowers our bills
levers.body: A fund that owns something useful “pays” its members as lower costs — power, internet, housing, food — instead of a dividend check.

precedents.name: Rural electric co-ops
precedents.fact: Private power companies wouldn’t wire farms — too few customers per mile. Neighbors formed nonprofit co-ops, and the 1936 Rural Electrification Act lent them the money to build.

precedents.name: Margins go back to members
precedents.fact: A co-op returns what it doesn’t need as “capital credits.” Since 1990, electric co-ops have returned nearly $13 billion to their members.

precedents.name: Arkansas’s co-ops
precedents.fact: Arkansas’s electric co-ops cover more than 60% of the state’s land and serve more than 1 million members, through 17 member-owned local co-ops.

precedents.name: One here already
precedents.fact: South Central Arkansas Electric Cooperative is headquartered in Arkadelphia. It was organized July 31, 1940, and serves parts of eight counties west and southwest of town.

precedents.name: Conway Corporation
precedents.fact: The City of Conway’s own not-for-profit utility company, incorporated in 1929 — electric, water, and cable and internet — with no profit motive, in its CEO’s words.

precedents.name: Paragould Light, Water & Cable
precedents.fact: Paragould’s city-owned utility: electric since 1938, water and wastewater added in 1984, cable in 1989.

precedents.name: Chattanooga’s EPB
precedents.fact: The city’s own electric utility launched the first community-wide gigabit fiber network in the U.S. in 2010. A University of Tennessee at Chattanooga study put the community benefit of the fiber network and its smart power grid at more than $5 billion since launch.

precedents.name: Champlain Housing Trust
precedents.fact: Founded in 1984 with the City of Burlington, Vermont’s support, to keep homes permanently affordable — the land stays in the trust, so each home stays affordable for the next family.

levers.here: Arkadelphia already owns its water and sewer system, paid for by rates, not taxes. Food is a household’s other big monthly bill — see the open-source grow units on the Grow-ops page.
levers.limit: Owning things means running them well: a utility or land trust needs good management, reserves for repairs, and customers who stay.

guardrails.lead: Elinor Ostrom won the 2009 Nobel Prize in economics “for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons.” She studied shared resources that people ran well for generations, and found eight things they had in common:
principles: Clear boundaries — who the fund belongs to, and what it’s for.
Rules that fit this place — written for local needs, not copied.
The people affected help make the rules.
Someone accountable checks — in the open.
Penalties start small and grow for repeat misuse.
Cheap, local ways to settle disputes.
Outside authorities respect the community’s right to run it.
For big shared resources, layers — local groups inside larger ones.

rules.text: A written purpose, set before the money arrives.
A spending rule — like Alaska’s 5% a year — so the fund outlives any one board or election.
Every deposit, loan, and payout on a public ledger anyone can check. This platform already keeps a hash-chained public record.
Residents decide the specific uses — a real, bounded pot, not a vote on the whole budget.

guardrails.warning: In 1994, Orange County, California’s treasurer borrowed against the county’s $7.6 billion investment pool to chase higher returns. It lost about $1.7 billion and the county filed for bankruptcy. A shared fund is safest when it is boring.

law.text: Arkansas counties and cities may invest spare money only in safe securities of five years or less, bank deposits, and similar — not stocks.
A new or higher local sales tax — including one dedicated to a fund — needs a vote of the people.
Arkansas’s Interlocal Cooperation Act lets local governments work together on shared services. Exactly how far it lets them lend to each other is an open question we’re checking.

residents: Put a use for shared money on the priorities board, and say why.
Watch what happens to it on What came of it — dated, cited, public.
Try the trade-offs yourself in the tax lab and on What if we saved?
Bring it to the body that decides — the calendar has the meetings.
limits: Shared funds can be mismanaged, raided, or spent on the wrong things. The safeguards above exist because that happens.
A dollar saved is a dollar not spent on something people need now. Every choice here is a trade.
Examples from other places show what’s possible, not what will work here. Each took years, local leaders, and often state or federal help.
None of this is a recommendation. It is a map of options, with the record of each.
